opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually one of the more underrated problems. People tend to assume that the hard part is getting the model to solve very difficult problems, like competition math or long agentic coding tasks, and the everyday stuff is "easy." But in practice, knowing *when not to think too much* is its own kind of intelligence.

If you ask a friend "what's a good place for lunch nearby," and they give you a ten-paragraph essay with caveats and a structured comparison, that's not a smart answer, it's a socially unaware one. A lot of current models, especially after heavy reasoning training, have this tendency. They've been rewarded for being thorough and careful, so they over-apply that behavior everywhere. The model doesn't really have a good sense of how much effort a question deserves.

So I see it as a calibration problem. You want the model to have something like an internal estimate: how hard is this question really, how much does the user care about precision versus speed, what's the cost of being slightly wrong here? Humans do this constantly without noticing. We answer most things instantly, and only slow down when we feel uncertainty or the stakes are high.

Technically, there are a few angles. One is on the training side: if your reward signals mostly come from hard, verifiable tasks, you implicitly teach the model that longer reasoning is always better. You need data and rewards that also value brevity and appropriateness, which is harder because "a good concise answer" is much less verifiable than "the right answer to a math problem." Another angle is adaptive compute, letting the model decide how much thinking to spend, rather than having a fixed mode. And then there's the product side: understanding the user's context, because the right length for the same question can be different for different people.

Honestly, I think this will matter more and more. As models get capable enough at the frontier tasks, the everyday experience, being fast, natural, not annoying, becomes what most people actually feel. It's a bit like the difference between a brilliant colleague and a brilliant colleague you actually enjoy working with.

r001.rationale: The response says everyday speed and concision are underrated while attention and rewards favor difficult, verifiable tasks and thorough reasoning, linking that imbalance to overlong everyday answers.

r002.rationale: It mentions difficult frontier tasks as a focus, but does not identify major U.S. AI companies as continuing to focus on raising AI intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually a much deeper problem than it looks. On the surface it sounds like a latency question, like can we make the model answer "what's the capital of France" in half a second instead of five seconds. But the real challenge is that the model has to decide how much to think before it starts thinking, and that's a kind of meta-cognition we don't train for very well.

Humans do this effortlessly. If you ask me what time it is, I don't go into some deep reasoning mode. If you ask me to prove a theorem, I do. We have this very fast, almost unconscious estimate of how hard a question is. Current models, especially the reasoning models, tend to be badly calibrated on that. You see them generating thousands of tokens of chain-of-thought for a question that a child could answer. And that's not just wasteful, it's actually a worse experience, because the user wanted a one-line answer and got an essay.

The way I think about it is that there are really two separate skills. One is the ability to reason deeply when needed. The other is knowing when not to. And historically we've been optimizing almost entirely for the first one, because that's what the benchmarks reward. Nobody gets a paper accepted for making the model say "Paris" faster. But if you look at actual usage, the overwhelming majority of queries are the simple kind.

So where does that go? I think the answer is partly about training signal. If your reward is only correctness, the model learns that more thinking never hurts, so it always thinks. You need the cost of thinking to show up in the objective somehow, whether that's explicit length penalties or user preference data that reflects people's impatience. And partly it's an agent design question, where the system itself decides which mode to route to. But honestly I'd prefer the model learn it internally, because routing is brittle and the model has much better information about its own uncertainty than some external classifier does.

There's also a subtle thing, which is that concise doesn't mean lazy. The hard part is being brief and still correct. A model that's confident and short and wrong is worse than one that's slow. So the real target is something like calibrated brevity, and I think that's going to be one of the more interesting research problems over the next couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response says research and optimization have focused on deep reasoning because benchmarks reward it, while speed and concise answers receive little priority.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is knowing how much effort a question deserves. If you ask an everyday question, you usually want a useful answer right away. You don’t necessarily want the model to explore every possibility or give you a long explanation.

But being concise is not simply generating fewer words. The model has to identify what you actually need, decide which details matter, and recognize when a short answer would leave out something essential. Sometimes that means one sentence; sometimes it means asking a clarifying question.

So I would frame the challenge as allocating effort appropriately. We want models that can think more when the problem requires it, but also recognize when they already have enough to answer. The goal is to use the right amount of computation and the right amount of language for the situation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is knowing how much thought a question actually needs. If you ask a simple everyday question, you probably want a direct answer in one or two sentences. But if the question is ambiguous or the consequences matter, spending a little more time can be worthwhile.

So conciseness isn’t just about generating fewer words, and speed isn’t just about generating words faster. The model needs to judge what you’re asking, what information you need, and when it has done enough. A short answer can require substantial reasoning behind the scenes. Ideally, we should evaluate whether the model helped you accomplish your goal, including how much time and attention it took from you.
